title: My Take On Micromanagement
author: Muth Martinez, Melissa
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that the word 'micromanagement' has become so broadly applied that it has lost its diagnostic power, obscuring the important distinction between legitimate oversight and control-driven surveillance. Her key move is to define micromanagement not by frequency of check-ins but by the nature and intention of the interaction: a manager who checks in daily in service of the work is not micromanaging; one who requires arrival confirmation is. The article locates the root of true micromanagement in an absence of trust, but -- crucially -- traces that absence upstream: individual managers are often symptoms of organisational systems that create the conditions for micromanagement, not sole causes. A senior leader who hovers produces direct reports who hover; a culture of lofty, poorly defined goals produces anxious control. The implication is that labelling someone a micromanager and moving on is organisationally insufficient -- the cultural and structural conditions that produced the behaviour must also be addressed. Muth Martinez closes by noting the consequences: micromanagement erodes autonomy, activates chronic stress responses, contributes to burnout and disengagement, and undermines the creativity and confidence that organisations most need.
points: Micromanagement is defined by the nature and intention of oversight, not its frequency: daily check-ins in service of the work and the person doing it are management; arrival confirmation for its own sake is control.

The word 'micromanager' has been applied so broadly -- including to entirely reasonable oversight -- that it obscures a real and harmful phenomenon, making it harder to diagnose and address genuine control problems.

True micromanagement is rooted in an absence of trust between manager and direct reports, but this trust deficit is within the manager's locus of control -- they shape the interactions and can choose to reshape them.

Micromanagement is rarely just a singular manager problem: a hovering senior leader creates hovering middle managers, and a culture of numerous, poorly defined goals creates the anxious oversight that individual managers then enact.

The organisational consequences are serious -- eroded autonomy, chronic stress, burnout, disengagement, and suppressed innovation -- and labelling someone a micromanager without addressing the systemic conditions that produced the behaviour will simply perpetuate the cycle.
quotes: Someone who checks in deliberately even daily in service of the work and the person doing it isn't micromanaging. However, a manager who checks in to confirm whether you've physically arrived at your desk most certainly is.

Micromanager has become one of those labels that tends to get applied so broadly that it's lost much of its meaning. Managers get called micromanagers for following up on deadlines, asking for status updates, or wanting visibility into how a project is tracking.

At the crux of this is a manager that does a whole lot more surveilling than supporting. If we're being honest, micromanagement is often rooted in an absence of trust between the manager and their directs.

Micromanagement undermines morale, engagement, confidence, and job satisfaction by eroding employees' sense of autonomy and ownership, stifling creativity and innovation, and activating a chronic stress response that, over time, contributes to anxiety, burnout, disengagement.
Labeling someone a micromanager and moving on is hardly a fix for anything. If the culture encircling them does not promote an alternate kind of conduct, the cycle will only sustain itself.
Responding to both realities proportionally is the only real way to mitigate the harmful effects of micromanagement in our organizational lives.
